words.verso:
Demonstrate the importance of interpersonal skills in the workplace.
Describe the manager's functions, roles, and skills.
Define organizational behavior (OB).
Show the value to OB of systematic study.
Identify the major behavioral science disciplines that contribute to OB.
Demonstrate why few absolutes apply to OB.
Identify the challenges and opportunities managers have in applying OB concepts.
Compare the three levels of analysis in this book's OB model.
words.note: This chapter lays the foundations of the whole Organizational Behavior course: from the manager's role to the three-level model of analysis used throughout the book.

words.verso:
Understanding OB helps determine manager effectiveness.
Leadership and communication skills are critical as a person progresses in his or her career.
Better interpersonal skills result in lower turnover of quality employees and higher quality applications for recruitment.
'Good places to work' have better financial performance.
words.note: Example: a company recognized as a 'great place to work' attracts talent more easily and retains it longer than a company known for toxic management.

words.verso: Someone who gets things done through other people in organizations.
words.note: Example: a store manager doesn't sell every item themselves; they coordinate a team of sales staff to hit the store's sales targets.

words.verso: A consciously coordinated social unit composed of two or more people that functions on a relatively continuous basis to achieve a common goal or set of goals.
words.note: Example: a company like Samsung, a charity, a professional sports team, or a government agency are all organizations.

words.verso:
Planning
Organizing
Leading
Controlling
words.note:
Example:
Planning = setting the quarter's sales target
Organizing = assigning tasks among the sales team
Leading = motivating the team through a tough period
Controlling = checking every week whether targets are being met.

words.verso: Mintzberg concluded that managers perform ten different, highly interrelated roles or sets of behaviors attributable to their jobs, grouped into three categories: interpersonal, informational, and decisional.
words.note:
Example: in a single day, a manager may:
represent the company at an event (interpersonal role)
pass information to their team (informational role)
decide how to allocate a budget (decisional role)

words.verso:
Figurehead: symbolic head, required to perform a number of routine duties of a legal or social nature.
Leader: responsible for the motivation and direction of employees.
Liaison: maintains a network of outside contacts who provide favors and information.
words.note:
Example:
a CEO cutting the ribbon at a store opening (figurehead)
giving a speech to motivate staff (leader)
regularly having lunch with business partners (liaison)

words.verso:
Monitor: receives a wide variety of information, serves as nerve center of internal and external information of the organization.
Disseminator: transmits information received from outsiders or from other employees to members of the organization.
Spokesperson: transmits information to outsiders on the organization's plans, policies, actions, and results.
words.note:
Example:
a manager who follows industry news (monitor)
relays a new policy to their team (disseminator)
answers a journalist's questions about company strategy (spokesperson)

words.verso:
Entrepreneur: searches the organization and its environment for opportunities and initiates projects to bring about change.
Disturbance handler: responsible for corrective action when the organization faces important, unexpected disturbances.
Resource allocator: makes or approves significant organizational decisions.
Negotiator: responsible for representing the organization at major negotiations.
words.note:
Example:
launching a new product (entrepreneur)
handling a surprise strike (disturbance handler)
approving an investment budget (resource allocator)
negotiating a contract with a supplier (negotiator)

words.verso:
Technical skills: the ability to apply specialized knowledge or expertise; all jobs require some specialized expertise.
Human skills: the ability to work with, understand, and motivate other people, both individually and in groups.
Conceptual skills: the mental ability to analyze and diagnose complex situations.
words.note:
Example:
Technical = an engineer who can write code
Human = a manager who defuses a conflict between two coworkers
Conceptual = an executive who anticipates how an economic downturn will affect the whole company

words.verso:
Luthans and his associates found that all managers engage in four managerial activities:
Traditional management
Communication
Human resource management
Networking
words.note:
Example:
Traditional management = drawing up the weekly schedule
Communication = running a team meeting
HRM = conducting an annual performance review
Networking = having lunch with a business partner

words.verso:
Successful managers (those promoted fastest) spend the most time networking (48%).
Effective managers (those with satisfied, high-performing employees) spend the most time communicating (44%).
Average managers spread their time more evenly across the four activities.
words.note: Example: a manager who climbs the hierarchy fast thanks to office politics isn't necessarily the one whose team performs best — being successful and being effective are two different things.

words.verso: Organizational behavior (OB) is a field of study that investigates the impact that individuals, groups, and structure have on behavior within organizations, for the purpose of applying such knowledge toward improving an organization's effectiveness.
words.note: Example: studying why team diversity boosts creativity, or how a manager's leadership style affects employee motivation, falls under OB.

words.verso: Behavior generally is predictable if we know how the person perceived the situation and what is important to him or her.
words.note: Example: an employee who perceives a reorganization as a threat to their job will tend to resist the change — a predictable behavior once you know how they perceive the situation.

words.verso:
Complements systematic study.
Argues for managers to make decisions based on evidence.
words.note: Example: instead of copying a trendy motivation technique, a company relies on studies showing which practices actually improve employee performance.

words.verso:
A gut feeling not necessarily supported by research.
Systematic study and EBM add to intuition, or those 'gut feelings' about why we do what we do; relying solely on intuition often means deciding with incomplete information.
words.note: Example: a manager who 'senses' an employee is about to quit, without having checked the actual signals (absenteeism, dropping performance, exit interviews...).

words.verso:
OB is an applied behavioral science built upon contributions from several disciplines:
Psychology and social psychology (individual and group level)
Sociology (group and organization-system level)
Anthropology (organization-system level)
words.note:
Example:
an individual motivation problem draws on psychology
a conflict between departments draws on sociology
a merger between a Japanese and an American company draws on anthropology (cultural differences)

words.verso: Psychology seeks to measure, explain, and sometimes change the behavior of humans and other animals.
words.note: Example: a work psychologist designs a selection test for hiring, or studies why an employee feels demotivated.

words.verso: Social psychology blends the concepts of psychology and sociology; it studies the influence people have on one another.
words.note: Example: studying why an employee changes their opinion in a meeting simply because the majority of colleagues think differently (group conformity).

words.verso: Sociology studies people in relation to their social environment or culture.
words.note: Example: comparing how the company culture of a startup differs from that of a government agency.

words.verso: Anthropology is the study of societies to learn about human beings and their activities.
words.note: Example: comparing attitudes toward hierarchy between a Korean company and an American company to adapt management style during an international merger.

words.verso: Situational factors that moderate the relationship between the independent and dependent variables — there are few, if any, simple and universal principles that explain organizational behavior.
words.note: Example: a highly directive leadership style works well in an urgent crisis, but becomes counterproductive with an experienced, autonomous team: the situation (contingency variable) changes the effect of leadership on performance.

words.verso:
Today's world of work offers a wide range of:
Categories of employment (employed, underemployed, entrepreneur, job seeking...)
Types of employment (full-time, part-time, flex-time, contingent...)
Places of employment (anchored office, floating shared space, virtual, work from home...)
Conditions of employment (local, expatriate, visa employee...)
Compensation for employment (salary, hourly, bonus, benefits...)
words.note: Example: a freelance consultant working remotely and paid hourly, versus a full-time expatriate employee with a fixed salary and benefits, illustrate two very different ways of being 'employed'.

words.verso:
In tough economic times, effective management is an asset.
In good times, understanding how to reward, satisfy, and retain employees is at a premium.
In bad times, issues like stress, decision making, and coping come to the forefront.
words.note: Example: during a recession, a company that manages employee stress well limits departures; in a strong growth period, it must focus on bonuses and training to avoid losing talent to competitors.

words.verso:
Increased foreign assignments.
Working with people from different cultures.
Overseeing movement of jobs to countries with low-cost labor.
Adapting to differing cultural and regulatory norms.
words.note: Example: a French manager sent to run a factory in Vietnam has to adapt their management style (more or less hierarchical, more or less direct) to local cultural norms.

words.verso: Organizations are becoming more heterogeneous in terms of gender, age, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, and inclusion of other diverse groups.
words.note: Example: a team made up of colleagues of different generations, nationalities, and backgrounds, which needs to be managed without imposing a single cultural mold.

words.verso:
Service employees have substantial interaction with customers.
Employee attitudes and behavior are associated with customer satisfaction.
Organizations need a customer-responsive culture.
words.note: Example: a call-center employee whose positive attitude toward their job directly translates into more satisfied, more loyal customers.

words.verso:
People skills are essential to managerial effectiveness.
OB provides the concepts and theories that allow managers to predict employee behavior in given situations.
words.note: Example: a manager who knows how to give constructive feedback without demotivating their team, based on what they know of each person's personality and expectations.

words.verso:
Networked organizations are becoming more pronounced.
A manager's job is fundamentally different in networked organizations.
Challenges of motivating and leading 'online' require different techniques.
words.note: Example: a fully remote team spread across several countries, coordinated only through Slack and video calls, with no shared physical office.

words.verso:
The creation of the global workforce means work no longer sleeps.
Communication technology has provided a vehicle for working at any time or any place.
Employees are working longer hours per week.
The lifestyles of families have changed — creating conflict.
Balancing work and life demands now surpasses job security as an employee priority.
words.note: Example: an employee answering work emails late at night because of a time-zone gap with colleagues abroad, at the expense of their personal life.

words.verso:
Creating a positive work environment can be a competitive advantage.
Positive organizational scholarship is concerned with how organizations develop human strength, foster vitality and resilience, and unlock potential.
This field of study focuses on employees' strengths versus their limitations.
words.note: Example: a company that holds sessions where employees share situations in which they performed at their personal best, rather than only discussing mistakes to fix.

words.verso:
Ethical dilemmas and ethical choices are situations in which an individual is required to define right and wrong conduct.
Good ethical behavior is not so easily defined.
Organizations distribute codes of ethics to guide employees through ethical dilemmas.
Managers need to create an ethically healthy climate.
words.note: Example: should a salesperson overstate a product's qualities to hit their sales target, at the risk of misleading the customer? That's a classic ethical dilemma.

words.recto: Three levels of analysis: the OB model
words.verso: This book's model analyzes organizational behavior at three levels — individual, group, and organization — through three stages: inputs, processes, and outcomes.
words.note: Example: at the individual level, personality (an input) influences decision making (a process), which in turn influences job performance (an outcome).

words.verso:
Defined as the variables like personality, group structure, and organizational culture that lead to processes.
Group structure, roles, and team responsibilities are typically assigned immediately before or after a group is formed.
Organizational structure and culture change over time.
words.note: Example: a team's diversity, a new employee's personality, or a company's culture at the time it was founded are all 'inputs'.

words.verso:
If inputs are like the nouns in organizational behavior, processes are like verbs.
Defined as actions that individuals, groups, and organizations engage in as a result of inputs, and that lead to certain outcomes.
words.note: Example: communication during a meeting, decision making when facing a problem, or resolving a conflict between two coworkers are all 'processes'.

words.verso: Defined as the key variables that you want to explain or predict, and that are affected by some other variables.
words.note: Example: an employee's performance, a team's stress level, or a company's survival are all 'outcomes' we try to understand from inputs and processes.

words.verso:
Attitudes: the evaluations employees make, ranging from positive to negative, about objects, people, or events.
Stress: an unpleasant psychological process that occurs in response to environmental pressures.
words.note:
Example:
an employee may have a positive attitude toward their salary but a negative one toward their manager
a project deadline that's too tight generates stress

words.verso: The combination of effectiveness and efficiency at doing your core job tasks is a reflection of your level of task performance.
words.note: Example: a salesperson who hits their monthly quota with a minimum of errors has good task performance.

words.verso: The discretionary behavior that is not part of an employee's formal job requirements, and that contributes to the psychological and social environment of the workplace, is called citizenship behavior.
words.note: Example: helping an overloaded coworker even though it's not your job, or suggesting an improvement without being asked to.

words.verso: Withdrawal behavior is the set of actions that employees take to separate themselves from the organization.
words.note: Example: being frequently late, taking unexplained absences, or ultimately resigning.

words.verso:
Group cohesion: the extent to which members of a group support and validate one another at work.
Group functioning: refers to the quantity and quality of a group's work output.
words.note:
Example:
a team whose members back each other up in front of management (cohesion)
who deliver a high-quality report on time (functioning)

words.verso:
Productivity: an organization is productive if it achieves its goals by transforming inputs into outputs at the lowest cost — this requires both effectiveness and efficiency.
Survival: the final outcome is organizational survival, simply evidence that the organization is able to exist and grow over the long term.
words.note:
Example:
a factory that produces more cars with less waste is productive
a century-old company still running today, like Coca-Cola, illustrates organizational survival

words.recto: The plan of the book: three levels of analysis
words.verso: The book organizes the whole study of organizational behavior around three levels — the individual, the group, and the organization — each broken down into inputs, processes, and outcomes, with a dedicated chapter for each topic.
words.note:
Example:
diversity in organizations (individual, ch. 2)
leadership (group, ch. 12)
organizational structure (organization, ch. 15)

words.verso:
Resist the inclination to rely on generalizations; some provide valid insights into human behavior, but many are erroneous.
Use metrics and situational variables rather than 'hunches' to explain cause-and-effect relationships.
Work on your interpersonal skills to increase your leadership potential.
Improve your technical and conceptual skills through training and staying current with OB trends like 'big data'.
Organizational behavior can improve your employees' work quality and productivity by showing you how to empower employees, design and implement change programs, improve customer service, and help employees balance work-life conflicts.
words.note: Example: instead of believing that 'younger employees are never loyal' (a generalization), a manager looks at their team's actual turnover data to understand and act on it.
